Dobson (Member): Mr. Bernard Price's paper contains an enormous amount of statistical information and interesting conclusions as a result of his experience on what may be regarded as a pioneer scheme of high voltage transmission of power generated on a large scale. Mr. Price and his staff have brought a wealth of information to the technical societies of the Witwatersrand, and they are to be sincerely congratulated in having overcome the enormous initial difficulties which are inherent to the inception of a large power scheme and in the elimination of most of the disastrous effects which accompany the characteristically severe lightning storms of the Witwatersrand. The attention given to the minutest details of organisation forms excellent reading, and no doubt has had a great effect on the achievement of satisfactory running of the system. In the words of the author, the paper reviews the scheme as a complete entity, it being pointed out that it would be impossible in a single paper to deal with the characteristics and behaviour of each individual class of apparatus. For this reason it is difficult to find points upon which comment or criticism is possible. articleTitle: Electric railway proposals in Great Britain
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: Remarkable activity is being shown by British railways in connection with the conversion of lines, especially in the neighbourhood of London, from steam to electric traction. The Great Eastern Railway Company, which carries an enormous volume of traffic from the city to the cast and north east of Loudon, has prepared a scheme of electrification and other improvements which will involve a capital of about £10,000,000. The London Brighton and South Coast Railway is bent upon electrifying practically the whole of its system between London and Brighton, and the “Underground” group in London has prepared a scheme for spending £6,000,000 on the development of its tube railways and allied transport services. The South Eastern and Chatham Railway has also made several plans for the conversion of its suburban system. One of the methods of propulsion laid before this country by a British engineer has some highly novel characteristics. It is proposed to propel the trains by means of internal combustion locomotives generating electricity, which in turn drives the motors on the locomotive or other parts of the train. The system is equipped with the usual overhead line or third rail which in this case, however, acts merely as a power interchange line. When a train is running down hill it returns current to the line, and when it is standing at a station the engine continues to run and to pump current into the interchange line. In this way additional power is afforded to trains which are ascending gradients or starting at stations. It is claimed for this system that it saves a large amount of capital expenditure and is very economical, especially on systems where traffic is not dense enough to justify the construction of large power stations and transmission mains.

articleTitle: The electrification of the chicago, milwaukee and St. Paul Railway
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: The purpose of this paper (perhaps better described as a lecture) is to bring to the knowledge and consideration of the Institute the engineering features of electrified sections of the Chicago, Milwaukee and St. Paul Railway in the United States. This electrification is remarkable in several respects. First, it is by far the largest and most important existing application of electricity to main line railway operation; second, it employs the highest direct current voltage thus far practically applied; and third, it employs for the first time successfully, and on a large scale, regenerative braking. Financial matters as regards first cost are only mentioned incidentally, because the costs of to-day and those of pre-war days are far apart, and little valuable and practical information could now be gathered from the actual costs of the system. Also, the financial results of the electrification are not stated, except with respect to power cost, because they are still unpublished history, locked in the archives of the railway company until time shall have winnowed all the facts. Suffice it to say that the ascertained economies are highly satisfactory to the owners, as evidenced by the recent decision to add greatly to the system as referred to later on. I might also add that the discussion of the engineering features is quite large enough for any one paper. But I hope to bring before you some of the considerations which lead to this great undertaking and to point to the causes of the economy which its owners confidently expect, and which experience has already indicated as amply assured.

articleTitle: Notes on aluminium
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: Ever since aluminium was produced in a commercial form, the greatest interest has been taken in its application to various engineering structures where lightness with strength is desirable. It was soon found that when aluminium was alloyed with other metals its strength was greatly increased without any great change in weight. Various alloys of aluminium have been used in the structure of airships and aeroplanes, and the results have been so promising that a special Committee was formed in Great Britain to undertake systematic research of the properties of aluminium alloys. A report recently issued by this committee embodies the results of seven years of research conducted in the National Physical Laboratory, which is subsidised by the British Government. This research has resulted in the discovery of many alloys which are of great promise for practically all kinds of engineering, particularly motorcar manufacture, railway rolling stock, internal combustion engines, and steam engineering. The only problem awaiting solution is the production of these alloys on a commercial scale. Already a beginning has been made in this direction by a British Government factory; and British manufacturers are looking closely into the possibility of producing some of these wonderful substances for regular use in place of steel.

abstract: Switch Tripping by Primary Batteries. — Mr Gould suggests that accumulators might be a more economical proposition for switch tripping than primary batteries. I am certainly not of this opinion, although of course one cannot say quite definitely without knowing the relative life of the two types of cell under the given conditions, and we have hardly had enough experience yet to settle this point. In the first place the first cost would be higher, as although I agree with Mr. Gould that considerably fewer accumulators would be used owing to their lower internal resistance, I do not consider the number could safely be reduced o the extent he suggests, because I think it would always be wise to have at least two sets of cells in parallel owing to the danger that one cell sulphating or otherwise badly deteriorating would practically put the battery out of action for switch tripping purposes if all the cells are in series. Secondly, I do not think Mr. Gould has realised what a big undertaking the periodical charging of some 80 odd batteries scattered all over the Reef would be. I judge from the fact that he mentions months and years in the same breath as the recharging period of modern accumulators when out of use. The question of charging monthly or yearly would make an enormous difference in the cost of maintenance.

abstract: (Associate Member): Mr. Adams bases his construction for the circle diagram on the full load stator current and maximum power factor — which is assumed to occur at full load. This latter assumption is rather a big one to make, as it is not often that such a condition holds good. The more difficult problem is to determine this power factor, and with ordinary instruments practically an impossibility, as about full load the variation of power factor is exceedingly small and cannot be determined in the ordinary way. A further requirement, surely, is the efficiency of the motor, but this seems to be neglected: without this, how can the performance of the motor be determined ? Unfortunately, no test figures have been given to show how this method agrees with test results.

abstract: Inception of the Scheme. — As one result of the war and consequent restriction of imports, the mining industry has found it to be imperative to utilise to the fullest extent all local resources in plant and material to supply its urgent necessities. Among the latter, obviously, stamp battery shoes and dies occupy a prominent place, a regular supply to the extent of about 7,500 tons annually being essential to the conduct of gold milling. Moreover, the Home Government requested South Africa, in common with the other Dominions, to make all possible metal manufactures locally and so lighten the task of the Home factories by releasing both metal and men for war purposes. Therefore, in order to consider the possibility of the manufacture of shoes and dies locally, a committee was appointed in February, 1916, at the instance of the Chemical, Metallurgical and Mining Society of South Africa, consisting of the following representatives of the Technical Societies of the Rand : Dr. W. This committee reported that it was of opinion that such manufacture was possible by utilising existing accumulations of scrap shoes and dies, and strongly recommended that it be undertaken at once, in view of increasing shortage and rapid rise in price. publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: (Associate Member): Mr. Price, on page 6, discusses the considerations which led to the location of the generating stations. There are not many suitable sites on or near the Witwatersrand for large generating stations, and hence there is little choice in the matter. The distribution of generating plant here, however, probably calls for more forethought than is the case when the power company is called upon to supply a purely, industrial area. The gold mines comprise nearly the whole of the power company's consumers, and the gold mining industry, is, as we all know, more speculative in its nature than what are known as industrial concerns. There is always a termination to the operations of a mine, and although there is no doubt that the mining industry will continue and even increase on the Witwatersrand for a good many years, the areas of greatest demand for energy will change. This being the case, what is now an ideal distribution of generating plant on the Witwatersrand may not be so favourable in a few years time. I do not suppose, for instance, that at the inception of the V.F.P. scheme the engineers could form any reliable opinion of the developments which we now know will take place on the eastern end of the Witwatersrand. For this reason, it is perhaps unfair to criticise the location of the stations and lay-out of the system. Mr. Price gives us the considerations which led to the selection of Vereeniging for the site of a generating station. Viewed from the standpoint which we now have, would it not have been better to have concentrated a much greater proportion of the plant on this site than is the case now ? As the centre of gravity of the load travels eastward, transmission losses with the present lay-out of the system will increase, and it is interesting to note that the furthest east consumer is very little further away from Simmerpan than it is from Vereeniging. Later on, again assuming that the present lay-out is permanent, the losses in transmitting power from Rosherville to where it is required will probably be as great as if it were transmitted direct from Vereeniging, where the cost of coal is less. It is true that as we get further east the freightage on coal from the Witbank Collieries becomes less, and if this were the only consideration, it would be better to increase the capacity of stations located on the east end of the system than to transmit from either Rosherville and Simmerpan or Vereeniging. Unfortunately, the water supply at the present time constitutes a difficulty, and taking all things into consideration, it appears to me that if the capacity at Vereeniging had been considerably increased and that at Rosherville correspondingly decreased, it would have resulted in more economical generation than is the case with the present lay-out.
